content.thinking:
I'm planning out the chopper's proportions—roughly 2.4m long, 1.1m tall at the handlebars, with wheel radii around 0.33m—and setting up the builder structure to construct it part by part.

Now I'm figuring out torus geometry orientation for the wheels (rotating them so the axle runs along X), sizing front and rear tires with different radii for a fat rear tire look, positioning the wheelbase with a raked front fork, and starting to lay out the frame and V-twin engine placement at the bike's center.

For the engine cylinders I'm angling them symmetrically in a V shape using rod shapes with finned rings, and setting up a mirroring helper to duplicate parts on both sides. I'm sketching the parts list, starting with tire paint using a dark gunmetal tone with an Overwatch-inspired orange accent for sidewall details.

I'm defining rims as steel toruses with radial spoke rods per wheel, cylinder hubs, and a solid rear disc with a panel-line torus for detail. Now I'm positioning the front fork at a raked angle with the head tube and front axle coordinates.

Adjusting the rake angle, settling on roughly 38.7° between the head tube and axle so it reads as a chopper-style fork, with the fork legs offset symmetrically and sliders made thicker than the upper tubes.

Still working out the fork and clamp geometry...

Mapping out the headlight lens and bezel geometry, then shifting to the frame structure—laying out the backbone, top tube, down tube, and engine cradle tube paths with their coordinates.

Now I'm continuing the frame geometry, defining the down tube path to the rear axle, then adding the rear stays, hardtail stays, and lower rails connecting the axle to the seat post and engine plate, before setting up the rear wheel width and axle position.

Shifting to the engine block, I'm placing the crankcase box with gunmetal and steel coloring, adding side cover discs with orange rings, then building the V-twin cylinders angled outward with finned cooling details and orange valve cover caps at the tips. I'm also starting the air cleaner assembly as a steel disc mounted between the cylinders.

Writing exhaust pipe paths...

Shifting to the fuel tank shape, I'll loft it as a teardrop using a series of elliptical stations defined by position, width, and height along its length.

I need to check that the tank's placement clears the top tube, nudging the tank's center down slightly so it sits just above the frame without an awkward gap, and plan mounting points. For paint, I'm thinking an orange base with a cream stripe running down the top centerline, defined by a thin band where the x-coordinate is near zero.

I'll skip toon shading since this needs a polished, Overwatch-style crisp look rather than a cartoon cel effect, and instead write a paint function that blends orange at the top of the tank into gunmetal/dark-blue lower down, with a zigzag transition line separating the two color blocks for a sharp, graphic edge.

Now I'm starting the seat geometry for a solo-rider seat, extruding a side-profile outline along the x-axis with points defined in z-y space relative to a pivot point.

I'm sketching a non-self-crossing seat outline with seven points, verifying the path doesn't cross itself, then placing the seat between z=-0.7 and -0.2 and checking how the rear fender covers it near z=-0.45.

Now I'm deciding on seat coloring and texture — using a dark leather grain paint function with gunmetal-brown tones, and considering orange piping or stitching along the seat edges for visual contrast.

Going with walls dark, faces orange for the simplicity. Now for the rear fender I'm sweeping an arc over the rear wheel using angled points at a fixed radius to position it, then applying an elliptical cross-section for the sweep geometry.

I'm realizing the fender might clash with the seat position—the fender top sits too high relative to where I placed the seat. I'll move the seat forward and shorten the fender arc's angular range so they don't overlap.

I'm adjusting the seat placement so it tucks closer to z -0.4 to 0.0, then shortening the tank stations to avoid overlapping the seat front, shifting the tank's z-range further forward.

Checking that the frame top tube passes cleanly under the seat without collision, then placing rear fender struts angling back from the axle plates to the fender top, and adding a glowing red taillight sphere at the fender's rear end.

I'm adjusting the fender arc angle range and placing the taillight box with a glow color, plus a license plate decal on a small plane. I'll skip a front fender since choppers often go without one, but I'm adding a front disc brake cylinder along the wheel axis.

Now I'm positioning the disc rotor with torus cutouts between the forks, then setting up the rear sprocket and engine pulleys with connecting belt rods running between their tangent points.

Next I'm placing forward-control footpegs, a kickstand reaching down to the floor with its foot pad touching at y=0.01, and double-checking that the tires' torus geometry sits flush with the ground. Finally I'm adding small front-end details like a mini speedometer gauge near the clamp.

Now I'm settling on the lighting accents: thin cables running from grips to the headstock, glowing underglow rods beneath the engine, and rim ring glows on the wheels. I decide to stick with one strong accent color—orange underglow (#ff9a2a)—paired with a warm white headlight and red taillight, rather than mixing in teal or cyan glows.

I'm also planning a decal for the tank—a symmetrical chevron graphic in cream and dark blue applied to the tank's surface, avoiding mirrored text to prevent rendering errors.

Now I'm working out the geometry of which direction the chevrons should point depending on which side of the tank they're on, tracing through the viewing direction and right-hand coordinate math for the +X and -X sides to make sure the chevrons visually point forward on each side.

I'm also planning engine details now—bolt rings around the gear cover using merged sphere geometries for the fasteners, and considering spoke rods for wheel rims using similar merging helpers.

Still writing wheel geometry logic...

Still figuring out color zones...

I'm positioning the gas cap slightly off-center to avoid the stripe, calculating where it sits on the tank's elliptical top surface around x=0.08, y≈1.085, z=0.22, sized as a small cylinder with a knob. I'm deciding to skip the oil tank detail since this is a hardtail with no rear shocks.

Now I'm shaping a sissy bar that sweeps up from the rear axle plates into a loop behind the seat, laying out a symmetric set of curve points on both sides that rise from around y=0.4 to y=0.98 before crossing over at the top, smoothed with a catmull spline.

I'm also checking that the bar stays just outside the fender edges at various heights, then adding a small tilted orange backrest pad box near the top of the sissy bar, plus noting I still need the rear wheel's tire width, axle nut, front brake caliper, and fork gaiter details.

For the handlebars, I'm plotting an ape-hanger path rising from the riser top up through a series of points to a max height around 1.4m, keeping it realistic for a chopper, then widening the grip ends with a slightly bigger orange sweep radius at the tips. I still need small mirror rods extending from the bar ends too.

Now I'm adding steel bar sections and orange grip sections using catmull-spline slicing, plus small brake/clutch lever rods angling forward from near the grip ends. I'm skipping detailed mirrors and rear brake pedal for now, planning flared tailpipes, and considering adding panel-line details and a belt guard cover to dress up the engine.

I'm settling on a color palette: dark gunmetal frame, orange tank/fender, cream accents, steel chrome highlights, navy and dark tire/rubber tones, plus glow and warning colors, keeping the total under 64 colors with paints handled separately. I'm skipping hex nut geometry for now and mapping out ground-contact heights -- tires at zero, footpegs and kickstand foot above that, exhaust around .28, and underglow around .2 -- to keep everything properly grounded.

Now I'm sketching out the wheel-building helper, deciding to represent tires as torus geometries rotated so their axis runs along X, with sidewalls detected by normal direction and a cream ring painted at a specific radius band for the tire detailing.

Since the tire torus surface sits right at the innermost radius, the rim itself would be hidden — I should instead add a visible lip ring offset slightly on the sidewall, around x=±0.03, so it actually shows from the side.

Calculating spoke positions for the front wheel using angular offsets around the rim, connecting rim points to a hub radius point for each spoke.

Adding the brake rotor with a darker inner ring for contrast, then defining the fork geometry with a curved profile function, thicker chrome slider sections lower down, and boot ribs as small torus rings along the upper fork.

Now I'm positioning the triple tree clamps, head tube, and frame joint, calculating precise coordinates where the head tube meets the frame tubes, and placing a spherical headlight housing in front of the fork legs.

I'm checking whether the lens disc sits flush against the headlight sphere's surface, finding a 17mm gap at the lens radius since the sphere curves inward faster than the flat circle plane -- so I need to adjust the lens placement to avoid floating.

Instead I'll use a small scaled sphere as the lens cap, positioned so it protrudes slightly beyond the housing tip, with a steel torus bezel wrapped around its base to make it read convincingly as a lens.

For the gauge, I'm positioning a tilted cylinder angled so its face points toward the rider, using a direction vector pointing up and back, with a glowing disc on its face to suggest a lit dial.

Now I'm defining the engine geometry: setting front and rear cylinder base points, computing their outward directions, building the cylinder bodies as rods, and adding a series of cooling fin discs spaced along each cylinder's length.

I'll move the pushrods outward past the fin radius so they're visible and chromed, then work out the air cleaner as a cylinder positioned between the V cylinders near the top.

Next I'll place the air cleaner off-center with a torus rim, perforated cream cap detail, and a connecting rod to the carb, then build the crankcase as a box positioned low enough to clear the tank, adding a smaller oil pan box beneath it.

Actually, the oil pan would collide with the frame's down tube cradle, so I'm dropping the pan and lowering the cradle tube instead to pass cleanly under the engine. For the side covers, I'm sizing cylinders to match the crankcase half-width, making the left side a larger steel primary belt cover with an orange ring accent and the right side a cam cover, both with bolt details, before moving on to the transmission box.

I'm placing the transmission box behind the crankcase with its own cover, verifying the z-ranges don't overlap, then adding engine and rear pulleys and working out the belt geometry connecting them, checking pulley radii and positions against the rear tire and plate placement so nothing clips.

I add the axle rod spanning the frame width, then realize the engine pulley and belt x-positions don't line up with the crankcase and cover geometry, so I shift the pulley out to x=0.19 beyond the primary cover to avoid the conflict.

Still working out pulley placement...

For the right side mirroring the cam cover setup, then I need to size the rear disc brake to nestle properly against the tire's inner radius, matching the disc radius against the tire's computed surface curvature at that cross-section.

Now I'm adding decorative detail to the disc face: concentric orange and cream rings via rotated torus shapes, plus hub cap cylinders and maybe spoke-like rods for visual texture.

Time to actually write the code now, keeping imports minimal and avoiding unused ones under strict TypeScript settings — pulling in three.js core, the builder, path utilities, texture/paint helpers, and BufferGeometryUtils for merging geometries.

I'm structuring the build function to return the baked root object, defining paint callbacks for the seat and tank with unused parameters prefixed by underscores, and adding a cream stripe detail to the tank.

Still refining the tank's zigzag boundary line between navy and cream, positioning it near the widest part of the tank sides and checking where decals might sit above that line.

I'm checking station width at that x position for the decal placement, then thinking about the rear plate — placing a small "CHOP 77" text plate near the fender end, working out its position and backing geometry at the tail of the sweep.

I'm computing the fender path points from θ=-70 to 28 for the catmull curve, and planning a small red glow box above the plate as a taillight accent near the fender's thin end.

For the sweep cross-section, I'm shaping a flat ellipse with 8 sides along the path's local frame, oriented so the wider axis runs sideways and the thinner one follows the curve's normal. For coloring, I'm defining a paint function that marks the outer edges cream, the center a thin navy pinstripe, and the rest orange to mimic a classic fender paint scheme.

Now I'm positioning the support struts—steel rods connecting the axle area up to points along the fender edge at specific angles, plus a second set of front stay struts at a shallower angle. Then I move to building the frame tubes using Catmull-Rom splines, starting with the top tube's control points running from the head tube down toward the seat area, while checking it clears the tank geometry properly.

I'm now tracing the down tube's path, with points curving from the head tube through the area near the crankcase to the swingarm pivot, adjusting radius for a thicker look near the base and considering how it threads past the engine block without clipping into the crankcase or cylinder geometry.

I'm plotting the rear stay rods connecting the axle plate up to the seat area, and separately mapping out the exhaust pipe's path from the cylinder head down past the engine, checking whether it clears the axle plate and rear fender width as it sweeps outward near the back wheel.

Checking clearance between the drag pipe at axle level and the belt guard's lower pulley position, I confirm the x-offsets keep them apart. I'm refining the rear pipe radius taper array to need at least three control points for a smooth gradient.

Now I'm placing the exhaust origin point relative to the front cylinder head and fin radius, nudging it slightly outward in x and z to clear the fin geometry, then sketching a heat shield as a constant-radius sweep over part of the pipe with a polished metal tone.

For the shield ribbing I'm skipping literal clamp bands or torus rings since they'd add mesh overhead, and instead using an alternating color function along the sweep parameter to fake a ribbed look cheaply. Now I'm starting on the exhaust tip flare, tapering the final radius outward for a flared end.

Still need to add a dark inner disc capping the exhaust pipe end to simulate a hollow tip, and I'm working out positioning for footpegs relative to the exhaust pipes and front wheel so they don't overlap, nudging coordinates to keep enough clearance.

Now I'm figuring out mounting rods connecting footpegs to the down tube, a kickstand foot assembly, and underglow rods beneath the engine, but these keep floating disconnected from the frame so I'm considering adding small support brackets or a belly pan instead.

I'm sketching a belly pan box under the engine with orange glow strips along its edges attached to the pan, then roughing out cable paths (clutch/brake lines) as curved sweeps from the handlebars down toward the tank and carburetor area, though the routing still needs refining so the cables don't pass through the tank geometry.

Now I'm adding mirror stalks extending up from the bar ends, capped with small flattened ellipsoid discs oriented to face rearward, keeping the overall height within the chopper's size limit. Skipping the front fender and fork brace for now, and leaving the tank cap and mounts as the next detail to add.

I'm also running through the full list of remaining components needed — springs, rear light, license plate, sissy bar, belt and pulleys, rotor, caliper, spokes, engine fins, valve cover, pushrods, air cleaner, pipes, oil pan, pegs, kickstand, grips, levers, cables, gauge, and headlight — while skipping tire text and extra decals for simplicity. I'm writing a helper function that builds a ring of bolt spheres around a center point by distributing them evenly along a circle and merging the geometries into one steel-colored mesh.

Now I'm setting up a batch of geometry helper functions: rods along arbitrary axes, boxes, cylinders oriented along X or arbitrary directions with adjustable segment counts, and a position function using Three.js vectors to offset along a normalized direction. I'm also defining a small fp function to compute frame points for curved parts, and starting to sketch out the wheel construction function.

Writing tire pattern code...

Still defining wheel geometry...

Rim will be steel with an orange tire stripe, 16 spokes up front, skipping the valve stem detail. I'll skip the spiral spring seat support and keep it simple for now. For final assembly I'm estimating around 200-250 parts, adding engine fin lines, bolts, rivets on the tank, and merged rivet rows along the rear fender edges for extra detail.

Computing rivet positions along the fender arc using angular spacing, placing small merged spheres at offset radii on both sides to simulate the rivet line. I'm skipping tank and seat rivets since those details are already handled, finishing the filler cap, then moving to the mirrors and finalizing the color scheme—gunmetal frame, steel fork, gunmetal engine with orange valve covers, and navy elsewhere.

Setting up the export metadata with style and commit info, then defining the tank loft using paint colors and elliptical station profiles. I'm writing the fender sweep using a catmull-rom path with flat end caps, then building the handlebar grips as a sweep split between a steel section and an orange grip section with flat caps at the ends.

For the levers, I'm computing rod endpoints off the bar path using vector offsets to position the steel lever rods. For the decal, I'm writing SVG chevron shapes with polygons in cream and navy colors plus a small rectangle, checking that each chevron polygon's points form a valid pointed shape.

Now I'm designing the license plate SVG with a rounded cream rect, navy border, and centered navy text, then reasoning about orientation -- since the plane faces -Z and is rotated 180° about Y, I'm checking whether the text reads correctly to a viewer standing behind it.

Checking imports and usage, I'll add a small point helper and a sphere helper for the vector rods before continuing to write the geometry code.

Working out the fin disc geometry and engine cylinder placement, making sure the pushrod and fin radii clear the crankcase bounds and sit at the right z positions.
